title: the Alvar hymns
hook: a singer carried into the temple looks at the Lord from the feet up

segments.voice: Yesterday opened the Alvar hymns with Kulasekhara, the king who asked to be a step at the shrine's door, low and still, facing the Lord. What could you see from the lowest seat? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-one.

Feet first. In the old custom of greeting an elder by touching their feet, the hand reaches down before the eyes ever meet. One Alvar's hymn runs on that same instinct. Tradition says its singer, Tiruppan, came from a community of bards kept outside the temple at Srirangam, and sang to the Lord from the riverbank. And it says a priest, Lokasaranga, was told by the Lord himself to carry the singer inside on his own shoulders. He did. Today, what Tiruppan sang when he got there.
screen: `FEET BEFORE FACE.` → `A SINGER KEPT OUTSIDE.` → `CARRIED IN ON A PRIEST'S SHOULDERS.`

segments.voice: The hymn is short, and it's named by its opening words, Amalanadipiran: the spotless one, the first Lord. What's remarkable is its path. Tiruppan stands before the image of Vishnu reclining at Srirangam, and he doesn't take it all in at once. He looks the way a devotee bows, starting at the feet. The holy feet, he sings, have come into my eyes. Then his gaze rises, one verse at a time. The red cloth at the waist. The navel, from which the lotus grows that holds the creator Brahma. The chest, where the goddess Lakshmi dwells. The throat. The red mouth. The long, wide eyes. And then the whole dark, beautiful form at once. It's a slow, loving look, the kind you'd give a sleeping child, taking in each part as if nothing else existed. Each part reminds him of a story, too: the throat that once swallowed the worlds, the hand that holds the discus. Then the last verse turns, and it's the line people remember. Having seen my nectar, he says, these eyes of mine will not look at anything else. The tradition says that with this song he merged into the Lord. Whether you read that as a miracle or as a poem's way of saying everything was complete, the hymn itself is the point. Notice who sings it. A man kept outside the walls is carried in and sings the hymn the temple keeps. In the Narada Bhakti Sutras, two days ago, there is no distinction among those who love, because they are his. Here, on a priest's shoulders, is that line acted out.
screen: `AMALANADIPIRAN: THE SPOTLESS ONE.` · `THE GAZE BEGINS AT THE FEET.` · `RISING, PART BY PART, TO THE EYES.` · `THESE EYES WON'T LOOK ELSEWHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a slow look. Choose something in front of you, an image you hold sacred if you have one, or a plant, or a face in a photo. Start at the bottom. Look only there for a breath or two. Then let the eyes rise, a little at a time, staying with each part before you move on. Don't rush to the whole. When you reach the top, take it all in at once and rest there. If you pray, you can let this be a way of beholding God. The bell holds the time.
The Alvar hymns. In Tiruppan's Amalanadipiran, a gaze that rises from the Lord's feet to his eyes and then won't look at anything else.
Your line: the Alvar hymns. Today, look at one person you love slowly, the way Tiruppan looked, as if seeing them for the first time. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: In Sri Vaishnava tradition, Tiruppan Alvar's Amalanadipiran is recited in daily worship, and devotees are taught to behold the deity in the temple from the feet upward.

original.note: Tamil āḻvār: the name the tradition explains as one sunk deep in God; Tiruppan is one of the Alvars.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymn praises God in general terms.
what it means: Tiruppan's hymn looks at the Lord at Srirangam from the feet upward, one part at a time, and ends with eyes that won't look at anything else.
what a scholar hears: amalan ādipirān, the opening words that name the hymn; Sri Vaishnava tradition reads the climb from feet to eyes as the devotee's place, beginning at the feet.

notes: Day 2 of the 'Alvar hymns' block. Days 1222–1225 (Tiruppavai, Tirukkovalur lamps, Tiruppallandu, Nammalvar and Nathamuni) were already on disk, and day 1220 took Kulasekhara; this day takes Tiruppan's Amalanadipiran. Year one (day 269) told the carrying story briefly; this day centers on the hymn's movement.

The order of the hymn's verses as given (feet; the red cloth at the waist; the navel and Brahma's lotus; the chest with Lakshmi; the throat; the mouth; the eyes; the whole form; the last verse) is from memory of the hymn and should be checked verse by verse. The waist-band verse is folded into 'the red cloth at the waist'.
Hook describes the custom of touching an elder's feet without claiming how widespread it is; confirm.

Tiruppan's community (pāṇar, bards) and his exclusion from the temple are stated as 'tradition says'. Confirm the framing is respectful and accurate, and that saying he 'merged into the Lord' matches the hagiography.
'Having seen my nectar, these eyes will not look at anything else' paraphrases the closing verse (en amudhinaik kaṇḍa kaṇgaḷ maṟṟonṟinaik kāṇāvē); confirm.
Tamil ஆழ்வார் (āḻvār): confirm spelling. Its gloss repeats the traditional explanation, not a lexicon etymology.

Editor pass: the hook now says the hymn (not the story) runs on the feet-first instinct, and 'the far bank of the river' is simplified to 'the riverbank'. 'The mouth that once swallowed the worlds' corrected to 'the throat': in the hymn the swallowing of the worlds belongs to the throat verse.
